front: きのうのパーティーは楽しかった＿＿。 (hearsay: something you heard)
back:
~そうだ (hearsay) — reports what you heard or read; no personal visual judgment involved. Attaches to the plain form of verbs / i-adjectives / na-adjective+だ / noun+だ.
Example: 天気予報によると、明日は雨が降るそうです。— "According to the weather forecast, it will rain tomorrow."

front: あの雲を見て。今にも雨が＿＿。 (visual judgment: how it looks)
back:
そうだ (様態, appearance) — "looks like / seems like," based on a visual or sensory impression. Verb ます-stem + そう; i-adjective stem + そう (いい→よさそう, ない→なさそう).
Example: この料理はおいしいそうです（見た目で）。— "This dish looks delicious (going by appearance)."

front: そうだ（様態）とそうだ（伝聞）の接続の違いは？
back: Appearance: verb ます-stem / i-adjective or na-adjective stem + そう (e.g. 降りそう, 寒そう). Hearsay: plain form + そう for everything (e.g. 降るそうだ, 寒いそうだ). Only the connection form changes — the meanings are completely different.

front: 彼は先生の＿＿。 (from outward appearance — the basis for the guess is what you observe)
back:
ようだ — a guess based on the speaker's own senses or overall situational judgment. Relatively subjective and indirect. Nouns take の+ようだ, na-adjectives take な+ようだ.
Example: あの人は日本人のようです。— "That person seems to be Japanese."

front: 彼は先生＿＿。 (a guess based on info heard from someone else — closer to hearsay)
back:
らしい — a guess based on objective information or hearsay. Carries less of the speaker's own subjectivity than ようだ. Connects to the plain form (na-adjectives and nouns attach directly + らしい).
Example: 天気予報では明日は晴れるらしい。— "According to the weather forecast, it'll apparently be sunny tomorrow."

front: ようだ・そうだ・らしい の根拠の強さを比べると？
back: そうだ (appearance) = based directly on a visual impression / ようだ = a guess combining the speaker's own senses and situational evidence / らしい = based on something heard from others or external information, somewhat objective and hearsay-like. All three can loosely mean "seems like / apparently," but the source of the evidence differs.

front: このケーキは食べる＿＿もったいない。 (too good to ~ / not quite worth ~ing)
back: ~には (もったいない/惜しい) — verb dictionary form + には + evaluation. "~するには" sets up a standard meaning "as a purpose/occasion for doing ~."

front: 彼女は思った＿＿優しい人だった。 (more ~ than expected / contrary to what one assumed)
back: ~より (surprisingly, more than expected) — "A は B より ~だ" shows the basis for a comparison. The pattern "~と思っていたより" (more than I thought) is also very common.

front: このかばんはあのかばん＿＿軽い。 (to the same degree as)
back: ~くらい / ~ほど + comparison. In affirmative sentences, くらい is more often used to show an equal degree (e.g. あのかばんくらい軽い — "as light as that bag").

front: 彼＿＿速く走れる人はいない。 (superlative in a negative sentence: nobody ~ as much as)
back:
~ほど…ない — noun + ほど + negative form, meaning "there's nothing more ~ than this," i.e. a superlative sense.
Example: 彼ほど頼りになる人はいない。— "There's no one as reliable as him."

front: 雨が降った＿＿、試合は中止になるだろう。 (hypothetical: if ~)
back:
たら — expresses an individual, concrete hypothesis, or a sequence of events that actually happens ("after doing ~"). Common in conversation.
Example: 家に帰ったら、電話します。— "I'll call you once/after I get home."

front: 安い＿＿、この店で買います。 (bringing up a topic and stating a condition based on it)
back:
"なら" — states a condition or piece of advice in response to something the other person said or brought up. Carries a strong nuance of "if that's what you're saying / if it's about ~."
Example: 京都に行くなら、清水寺がおすすめです。— "If you're going to Kyoto, I'd recommend Kiyomizu-dera."

front: 毎日練習すれ＿＿、上手になります。 (a general, inevitable cause-and-effect relationship)
back:
ば — expresses a general rule or a constant conditional relationship, or the "the more you do X, the more Y" pattern. The most general and objective of the conditional forms.
Example: 水は0度になれば、氷になる。— "Water turns to ice once it reaches 0 degrees."

front: なら・たら・ば の使い分けの基本イメージは？
back: たら = an individual hypothesis or a time sequence ("after doing ~") / なら = a condition or piece of advice responding to a topic already raised / ば = a general rule or constant condition, common in proverb-like expressions. Even though all three can mean "if," the perspective differs.

front: このパン、焼きたてで温かい＿＿おいしい。 (precisely because ~ / to a degree that justifies the result)
back:
~だけあって / ~だけに — emphasizes that a result is fitting given a certain attribute or status.
Example: さすが留学経験があるだけあって、英語が上手だ。— "As you'd expect from someone with study-abroad experience, their English is good."

front: 彼は疲れているの＿＿、笑顔を絶やさなかった。 (contrast/surprise: even though ~)
back:
のに — a contrastive expression showing a result that goes against expectations. Often carries the speaker's nuance of surprise or dissatisfaction.
Example: あんなに勉強したのに、試験に落ちた。— "Even though I studied that much, I failed the exam."

front: 彼は疲れている＿＿、笑顔を絶やさなかった。 (simple contrast: but ~)
back: けど / けれど(も) — a simple contrast/concession. Unlike のに, it carries little of the speaker's surprise or dissatisfaction and is more neutral.

front: のに と けど の一番の違いは？
back: のに = often includes surprise, dissatisfaction, or shock at a result that differs from what was expected / けど = a plain contrast of facts with little emotional nuance. Used alone at the end of a sentence, "のに！" can itself express dissatisfaction.

front: 無理な＿＿しなくてもいいですよ。 (nominalizer: こと)
back: ~こと — a formal noun that nominalizes verbs and adjectives. Used to refer to abstract or general matters.

front: 彼が歌っている＿＿を見た。 (a concrete scene perceived directly by eye or ear)
back:
~の — a formal noun used to point to a concrete event that can be directly perceived. Pairs well with verbs like 見る (see), 聞く (hear), 手伝う (help).
Example: 子供が公園で遊んでいるのを見た。— "I saw the child playing in the park."

front: 「の」と「こと」使い分けの基本ルールは？
back: Perception verbs like 見る, 聞く, 手伝う + a concrete scene = "の." Hobbies, goals, general matters, and verbs like 話す, 伝える, 決める = "こと." Fixed idiomatic patterns like "~ことができる" always use こと.

front: 彼が来る＿＿は分からない。 (uncertainty, no question word: a yes/no-type unknown)
back:
~かどうか — used to turn a yes/no question into a noun clause (add どうか after か).
Example: 彼が来るかどうか分からない。— "I don't know whether or not he's coming."

front: 彼がいつ来る＿＿は分からない。 (unknown content that includes a question word)
back:
~か — when a sentence contains a question word (いつ, どこ, だれ, 何), use か alone to nominalize it (どうか isn't needed).
Example: 彼がいつ来るか分からない。— "I don't know when he's coming."

front: 今度こそ合格＿＿と決めた。 (a decision made by one's own will)
back:
~ことにする — expresses a decision made by one's own will. Carries the nuance of "I decided (of my own accord) to ~."
Example: 来年、留学することにした。— "I decided to study abroad next year."
tag: ことにする_vs_ことになる

front: 会社の都合で、大阪に転勤する＿＿。 (not one's own decision — determined by outside circumstances)
back:
~ことになる — expresses that something was decided or came about not by one's own will, but by circumstances or someone else's decision.
Example: 来月から新しい部署で働くことになりました。— "It's been decided that I'll work in a new department starting next month."
tag: ことにする_vs_ことになる

front: ことにする と ことになる の主語の違いは？
back: ことにする = a proactive, self-initiated decision (I decided it myself) / ことになる = an objective decision or outcome (came about through outside factors, rules, or the natural course of events). "ことになっている" is an extended form used for rules or habitual practices.
tag: ことにする_vs_ことになる

front: このドアは風で＿＿。 (intransitive verb: the subject itself changes; no agent is mentioned)
back: Intransitive verbs like 開く (あく, "to open") — focus on the result or change of state itself. Best memorized in pairs with their transitive counterparts (開く/開ける, 閉まる/閉める, 壊れる/壊す, etc.).

front: 彼が窓を＿＿。 (transitive verb: an agent acts on an object)
back: Transitive verbs like 開ける (あける, "to open [something]") — express an agent intentionally acting on an object. Takes the form "~を + transitive verb."

front: 自動詞と他動詞、状態を表したい時に使う「てある」はどちらと結びつく？
back: 他動詞 (transitive) + てある = "it's in a state of ~ (as a result of someone's deliberate action)." 自動詞 (intransitive) + ている = simply "it's in a state of ~." (e.g. ドアが開いている "the door is open" vs. ドアが開けてある "the door has been left open [by someone].")

front: 先生に息子をほめられた。 (___ passive: a nuance of being inconvenienced or bothered)
back:
間接受身 (indirect passive / nuisance passive) — a passive form where the subject is a person indirectly affected by an action, whether the verb is transitive or intransitive. Distinctively Japanese, and usually carries a nuance of "it was a problem / I didn't like it."
Example: 夜中に赤ちゃんに泣かれて、眠れなかった。— "The baby cried [on me] in the middle of the night, and I couldn't sleep."

front: 私は先生に名前を呼ばれた。 (___ passive: directly the target of the action)
back: 直接受身 (direct passive) — the most basic passive, where the person directly affected by the action becomes the subject as-is. Takes the form "A は B に(を) ~される."

front: 新しい図書館が来年建て＿＿予定です。 (a passive where the agent isn't stated and a thing is the subject)
back:
られる (agentless / inanimate-subject passive) — used to state a fact or event objectively without naming the agent. Common in news and explanatory writing.
Example: このビルは1990年に建てられました。— "This building was built in 1990."

front: 直接受身・間接受身（迷惑）・無生物主語の受身の違いを一言で？
back: Direct = you were directly affected by something / Indirect (nuisance) = you were indirectly, often negatively, affected by someone else's action / Inanimate-subject = the agent is left vague to state a fact or event objectively. Japanese passives often carry a stronger sense of "being affected/harmed" than English ones.

front: 友達が引っ越しを手伝って＿＿。 (the speaker's side receives an action from someone; viewpoint = self)
back:
くれた — someone does something for the speaker (or the speaker's in-group). The person performing the action is the subject; the one who benefits is the speaker's side.
Example: 友達が手伝ってくれた。— "My friend helped me [out of kindness]."

front: 私は友達に荷物を持って＿＿。 (the speaker gets someone to do something (by asking); the beneficiary is the subject)
back:
もらった — the speaker (or their in-group) has someone else do something for them. The beneficiary is the subject.
Example: 私は友達に手伝ってもらった。— "I had my friend help me."

front: 私は友達に本を貸して＿＿。 (the speaker does something for someone else; the giver is the subject)
back: あげた — the speaker (or their in-group) does something for someone else. The one performing the action is the subject. Use さしあげる for social superiors and あげる for equals/subordinates — using あげる directly toward a superior can easily sound rude, so be careful.

front: あげる・もらう・くれる の視点の違いをまとめると？
back: あげる = me → someone else (the giver is the subject) / もらう = me receiving from someone else (the receiver is the subject) / くれる = someone else → me (the giver is the subject, but the benefit flows to me). くれる always presupposes that the speaker, or someone in the speaker's in-group, is the beneficiary.

front: 今にも泣き＿＿な顔をしていた。 (on the verge of ~ing / looking like it's about to happen)
back: ~そうな (appearance-そうだ + noun modifier) — verb ます-stem + そう + な + noun, meaning "a look/state that seems about to ~ any moment now."

front: 彼はこの仕事に慣れて＿＿ようだ。 (~てきた: shows a change that has gradually progressed)
back:
~てきた — expresses a change or continuation from the past leading up to the present. Best memorized as a pair with ~ていく (change from the present into the future).
Example: 日本語が話せるようになってきた。— "I've gradually become able to speak Japanese."

front: これから状況はもっと悪くなって＿＿だろう。 (change from the present into the future)
back: ~いく — "~ていく" expresses a change or continuation heading from the present into the future. Pairs with てきた (past → present).

front: このレポートは明日までに書か＿＿ばならない。 (obligation)
back: ~なければならない / ~なくてはいけない — the basic forms for expressing obligation or necessity. Often contracted in conversation to なきゃ or なくちゃ.

front: 急いでいるので、先に帰っ＿＿もいいですか。 (asking for permission)
back: ~てもいい / ~てもかまわない — expressions for asking for or granting permission.

front: 一人で＿＿ようになった。 (~できるようになる: a change in ability)
back: ~できるようになる — expresses becoming able to do something you couldn't do before; a change in ability or state. "~ようになる" can be used broadly for any change in state or habit (e.g. 野菜を食べるようになった — "I've started eating vegetables [as a habit change]").

front: このワインは古ければ古い＿＿おいしくなる。 (the more you ~, the more ~)
back:
~ば~ほど — a compound expression meaning "the more you do ~, the more [a degree] increases."
Example: 練習すればするほど上手になる。— "The more you practice, the better you get."

front: 彼女は疲れている＿＿、休もうとしなかった。 (~ながらも: contrast/concession)
back: ~ながら(も) — expresses a contrast meaning "even though ~" (same usage as ~つつ). Distinguish from the simple-connective ~ながら (simultaneous actions).

front: 新製品の発表会は来週行われる＿＿。 (~予定だ: a formal/official plan)
back: ~予定だ / ~こととなっている — formal expressions for a plan or arrangement. Close in meaning to "ことになっている," used for rules or conventions.
tag: ことにする_vs_ことになる

front: 彼は独身だ＿＿聞いていたが、実は結婚していた。 (quoting something heard secondhand)
back: ~と聞いていた / ~と(いう)話だ — a form for quoting hearsay information. Similar to そうだ (hearsay), but used when you want to make the source of the information more explicit.

front: アンケートによると、七割の人が賛成＿＿。 (~という結果だ: reporting a survey result)
back:
~という結果だった / ~そうだ — a set pattern, "~によると~そうだ," for reporting hearsay information based on a survey or data.
Example: アンケートによると、七割が賛成だったそうだ。— "According to the survey, apparently 70% were in favor."

front: 彼は宝くじに当たった＿＿、贅沢な暮らしはしていない。 (~割には: surprisingly, considering ~)
back: ~割には — expresses a gap between the degree expected from a premise and how things actually turned out.

front: どんなに疲れていても、彼は毎朝ジョギングする＿＿だ。 (~ことにしている: a self-imposed habit)
back: ~ことにしている — expresses something you decided for yourself and continue as a habit (the continuous/habitual version of ことにする).
tag: ことにする_vs_ことになる

front: 道に迷った時は、人に聞け＿＿いい。 (~ばいい: advice)
back: ~ばいい / ~たらいい — set expressions for advice or suggestions, meaning "it would be good to ~."

front: 田中さんという＿＿人が訪ねてきました。 (~という: a quotative use for introducing a name or piece of content)
back: ~という — a quotative expression used to introduce a name or piece of content. "~という + noun" means "called ~ / that goes by the content ~."

front: 向こう＿＿見えるビルが、私の会社です。 (that side over there — a demonstrative that presupposes a shared viewpoint between speaker and listener)
back: あちら／あそこ（こそあど）— refers to a place far from both the speaker and the listener. Organize こそあど as: speaker's reference point (こ), listener's reference point (そ), far from both (あ), unknown (ど).

front: そういえば＿＿、彼から連絡があったんだった。 (an expression for suddenly recalling something related to the topic)
back: そういえば — used when something related suddenly comes to mind in the flow of conversation ("come to think of it").

front: 名前、何だった＿＿。 (~だっけ: a casual way of confirming something you can't quite recall)
back: ~っけ — a casual expression used when trying to recall or confirm something you've forgotten. Most often appears as "~だったっけ？".

front: このホテルは駅から近い＿＿、部屋も広くていい。 (listing multiple good reasons: ~し、~し)
back: ~し、~し — a connective that lists reasons or facts in parallel. Used to bundle multiple pieces of evidence together to strengthen a claim.

front: みんな忙しい＿＿、パーティーは延期しよう。 (~ことだし／~ことだから: stating a reason indirectly/softly)
back: ~ことだし / ~ことだから — expressions that state a reason in a roundabout, softened way.

front: 彼女はまるで女優の＿＿きれいだ。 (まるで～ようだ: an emphasized metaphor)
back: まるで~ようだ — a set pairing of the emphasizing adverb まるで ("just like") with ようだ. A strong metaphor: "it's not actually so, but it looks/feels exactly like it."

front: 台風が近づいている＿＿、風が強くなってきた。 (~せいか: guessed as a possible cause)
back: ~せいか — a reason expression that includes a guess: "maybe it's because of ~, though it's not certain." Usually used for negative outcomes (use ~おかげか for positive ones).

front: 今日は早く起きた＿＿、頭がすっきりしている。 (おかげで: the reason for a good outcome)
back: ~おかげで / ~おかげか — expresses the reason for a positive outcome (as opposed to ~せいで, which is negative).

front: 彼の話は本当か嘘か、＿＿にしても面白い。 (~にしても: concession — either way)
back: ~にしても — expresses a concession meaning "even if ~." Nearly synonymous with ~としても.

front: どんなに安くても、必要ない物は買わない＿＿。 (たとえ~ても: a strong concession with an extreme hypothetical)
back: たとえ~ても — a strong concession expression: "even supposing an extreme situation, ~ still holds." Often paired with どんなに~ても.

front: これさえあれば、他に何もいらない。 (~さえ~ば: the bare minimum condition)
back: ~さえ~ば — emphasizes a necessary-and-sufficient / minimum condition: "as long as you have just this, that's enough."

front: 必ずしも高い物がいい物だ＿＿限らない。 (~とは限らない: partial negation)
back: ~とは限らない — expresses a partial negation: "that's not necessarily always true." Often paired with 必ずしも ("not necessarily").
